citation.title: Multi-material Multi-physics Topology Optimization with Physics-informed Gaussian Process Priors
citation.authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Amin Yousefpour, Ramin Bostanabad
citation.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.LG); a version of record is also registered at Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
citation.version_coded: arXiv v1 (19 Feb 2026; only version on the abs page), full text, tables and figures read from the PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.17783). The journal DOI (10.1016/j.cma.2026.119163) redirects to linkinghub.elsevier.com then sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045782526004366, which returned HTTP 403 to scripted access; the version of record was not read (no bypass attempted).

included.reason: I-QUALITY (full-text determination; this blind second-pass coder has no access to the original title/abstract screening code)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: For 2D multi-material compliance minimization on four canonical benchmarks (MBB, cantilever, bridge, L-shape) under a mass-only constraint, PIGP's median FEM compliance is about 7-11% higher (worse) than ordered SIMP and PolyMat, which the authors call slightly higher yet comparable.
claim.key_phrase: achieves compliance values that are slightly higher yet comparable
claim.location: Section 4.1, Table 4 (p. 24-25); first main-text quantitative comparison with a classical method. The Abstract, Conclusion and Introduction contain no quantitative classical-method comparison (only qualitative statements)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: No speed, runtime or cost comparison with a classical method is quantified anywhere in the article. The Conclusion states, qualitatively and with no numbers, that PIGP training cost is higher than SIMP's ('it comes at the expense of higher training costs compared to methods such as SIMP') and that COMSOL is 'slower' than PIGP. Neither statement gives a number, so no speed-up is derivable.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 4.2, Table 8 (heat conduction): PIGP has lower (better) median thermal compliance than SIMP in the single-material 2D and 3D cases (1.775 vs 1.986; 25.421 vs 29.954) but higher (worse) in the multi-material 2D case (0.577 vs 0.487). (2) Sec. 4.3, Table 11 (compliant mechanism): PIGP's median output displacement is consistently lower (worse) than ordered SIMP in both examples and both material settings. (3) Sec. 4.4, Table 15 (thermo-mechanical vs COMSOL): PIGP's median output displacement is higher (better) than COMSOL for the single-material actuator and gripper (21.88 vs 18.23; 16.61 vs 13.47). (4) Qualitative Abstract/Conclusion framing: 'comparable' objective values to open-source codes, higher training cost than SIMP, COMSOL 'slower' and needing fine-tuning.

baseline.classical_method: Ordered SIMP (OC-type update, no projection filter, for a fair comparison) and PolyMat (polygonal-FE density TO) for the 2D CM/heat-conduction/compliant-mechanism benchmarks; a single-material SIMP 3D implementation (Liu & Tovar) for 3D CM/heat-conduction; COMSOL with a global MMA optimizer and a three-stage beta-continuation projection for the thermo-mechanical benchmarks
baseline.implementation: Open-source SIMP and PolyMat codes (refs [22, 23, 73]); commercial COMSOL, with ABAQUS used to FE-verify the binarized thermo-mechanical designs from both COMSOL and PIGP (Sec. 4.4)
baseline.solver: not stated (open-source SIMP/PolyMat and COMSOL FE solvers; solver class - direct vs iterative - is not named)
baseline.hardware_classical: Intel Core i7-11700K CPU (Sec. 4, p. 28: 'All simulations based on SIMP, PolyMat, and COMSOL are run on an Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-11700K CPU')
baseline.hardware_ml: NVIDIA A100 GPU (same locator: 'Our framework is implemented in Python and executed on an NVIDIA A100 GPU')
baseline.problem_size: 2D CM: SIMP/PolyMat meshes 14,701-45,413 FE nodes, PIGP fine collocation grids up to (401,201) (Table 3); 3D CM: SIMP3D FE nodes up to (77,39,27), PIGP fine CPs up to (92,47,32) (Table 3); heat conduction: 2D up to (401,201), 3D up to (81,41,41) (Table 7); thermo-mechanical: COMSOL/PIGP FE nodes (135,68)-(277,139) (Table 14)
baseline.classical_iterations: not stated for SIMP or PolyMat (no iteration count or numerical stopping tolerance given anywhere in the text, searched throughout); COMSOL uses a stated 3-stage beta-continuation (beta in {8,12,16}), 500 iterations per stage = 1,500 iterations (Sec. 4.4)
baseline.classical_time: not stated (no wall-clock or runtime number is reported for SIMP, PolyMat or COMSOL anywhere in the article)
baseline.ml_time: not stated (PIGP training is reported only in epoch counts - up to 10,000 epochs for CM/heat-conduction/compliant-mechanism, 20,000 for thermo-mechanical, Sec. 4.1-4.4 - never in wall-clock time)
baseline.training_time: not stated; only epoch counts are given (see ml_time). PIGP is trained from scratch per problem instance (Sec. 3), so there is no separate offline training phase distinct from the reported per-case runs
baseline.data_generation_cost: not applicable: PIGP uses independent GP priors with NN mean functions optimized per problem instance from a physics-based loss; no labeled training dataset is generated or used (Sec. 3)
baseline.quality_metric: FEM-computed compliance (CM, heat conduction) or output displacement (compliant mechanism, thermo-mechanical) of the final topology from every method, reported as median/mean/std over 10 independent random-initialization runs (Tables 4, 5, 8, 11); thermo-mechanical designs are additionally binarized and FE-verified in ABAQUS (Sec. 4.4, Table 15). Mass/cost constraint satisfaction is reported alongside every objective value
baseline.quality_gap: Table 4 (primary outcome), mass-only constraint, median compliance PIGP vs ordered SIMP: MBB 1.049 vs 0.982 (+6.8%), cantilever 0.976 vs 0.890 (+9.7%), bridge 1.133 vs 1.041 (+8.8%), L-shape 3.529 vs 3.194 (+10.5%) [all derived]; PIGP is consistently higher (worse) by roughly 7-11%, described by the authors as 'slightly higher yet comparable'

R1.evidence: Table 2 and Table 4: both methods target the same mass/cost fraction and are scored by the same FEM evaluation of the returned topology, so the quality comparison itself is on a common metric and constraint target. But the match is loose: (a) the classical (SIMP/PolyMat) iteration count or numerical stopping tolerance is never stated anywhere in the article (searched throughout), so it cannot be confirmed the classical baselines were run to a comparable stopping point as PIGP's fixed epoch budget; (b) Table 3 shows PIGP's fine collocation grid (e.g. 401x201 CPs) is finer than ordered SIMP's FE mesh (301x151 nodes) for the same 2D CM benchmarks, an unmatched resolution/budget between the two sides.

R2.evidence: The primary outcome (Table 4) compares design quality only; no runtime, speed or cost claim against SIMP/PolyMat is made for this outcome, so the efficiency criteria (a)-(e) do not bear on it. For the record: classical runs use an Intel i7-11700K CPU while PIGP uses an NVIDIA A100 GPU (Sec. 4), with no stated justification, but this asymmetry is not tied to any speed claim here.

R3.evidence: No speed or cost claim against a classical method is made anywhere (see claimed_speedup_basis). Independently, PIGP is a per-instance SAND framework optimized from scratch for each problem via independent GP priors with NN mean functions (Sec. 3); there is no offline training on a labeled dataset and no separate data-generation phase, so any training/compute cost sits inside R1/R2 rather than needing separate cost accounting.

R4.evidence: Sec. 4.1-4.4, Tables 4/5/8/11/15: the returned topology from every method (including PIGP) is independently FE-verified (FEM, or ABAQUS for the thermo-mechanical case after binarization), and mass/cost constraint values are reported alongside every objective value across 10 runs. However, no systematic failure or infeasibility rate (disconnected material, floating material, volume violation) is reported; the only related disclosure is a one-off qualitative note that '10k training epochs was insufficient for this example' for the multi-material displacement inverter (p. 32), not a counted rate.

reporting.n_test_cases: 10 distinct benchmark geometries across four problem classes: 4 CM benchmarks (MBB, cantilever, bridge, L-shape; each 2D+3D, single/multi-material, mass/cost/(mass,cost) constraints, Sec. 4.1), 2 heat-conduction benchmarks (2D+3D, single/multi-material, Sec. 4.2), 2 compliant-mechanism benchmarks (displacement inverter, gripper; single/multi-material, Sec. 4.3), 2 thermo-mechanical benchmarks (actuator, gripper; single-material vs COMSOL plus 2 multi-material combinations, Sec. 4.4)

notes: As a blind second-pass coder I have no access to the original title/abstract screening file, so the 'I-QUALITY' reason above reflects only my own full-text determination, not a confirmation of the original screening code. Primary-outcome search: the Abstract has no quantitative classical comparison ('super-resolution topologies', 'validate using open-source codes and COMSOL' are qualitative); the Conclusion likewise only states qualitatively that objective values are 'comparable' and that training cost is higher than SIMP's; the Introduction's only quantitative runtime figure ('Jeong et al. [61] reported an average runtime of four hours', p.3) is a comparison between two ML methods, not with a classical method. The first main-text quantitative classical comparison is Table 4 (Sec. 4.1), which is taken as the primary outcome per protocol Sec. 5.1 step 2. No article-wide speed/cost claim against a classical method exists (searched the full text for hour/minute/second/GPU/CPU/speedup/faster/slower - the only hits are the per-hardware statement in Sec. 4 and the qualitative Conclusion remarks already quoted), which is why R2 and R3 are both na for this quality-stratum primary outcome. Code: the PDF's page-1 'GitHub Repository' hyperlink points to https://github.com/Bostanabad-Research-Group/ (an organization page, not a specific repo); that org page lists a repository named 'MM-TO' - 'Multi-Material and Multi-physics Topology Optimization' - whose README (checked 2026-09-24) names this exact paper and title. The repo is public with 9 commits, an MIT licence, and folders for every example in Sec. 4.1-4.4, though it contains PIGP code only (no SIMP/PolyMat/COMSOL baseline code); the article text itself says code is 'accessible via GitHub upon publication' (future tense), so the repository apparently went public after or around submission. retest_candidate is true because the ML side is public and runnable and the cited classical baselines (refs [22] ordered SIMP, [23] PolyMat, [73] SIMP 3D/Liu-Tovar) are themselves standard, separately published open-source codes, even though not bundled in this repo; the required hardware (one NVIDIA A100 GPU) is stated. No author of this article is named Jun Wang (authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Amin Yousefpour, Ramin Bostanabad); reference [4] (Wu et al.) cites a 'Wang, J.' as a co-author of a different, unrelated paper in the bibliography, not as an author of this article. Duplicates: pool.csv holds a single combined record for P00019 carrying both the arXiv id (2602.17783) and the journal DOI (10.1016/j.cma.2026.119163); no separate duplicate pid for this title was found, so FT-DUPLICATE does not apply.
